title: The past conditional
why: After hypotheses about the present (si tuviera…), the learner learns to talk about what could have happened: habría + participle for regrets, reproaches and the future in the past (dijo que vendría). The lesson stops short of “if I had known” (level B2) and prepares the pluperfect in the next lesson.

Habría + participle: I would have done

The past conditional is built just like English “would have done”: the auxiliary in the conditional, then the past participle. The auxiliary is always haber, with the conditional endings you know: habría, like tendría or podría.

haberexample: ir
yohabríahabría ido
túhabríashabrías ido
él, ella, ustedhabríahabría ido
nosotros, nosotrashabríamoshabríamos ido
vosotros, vosotrashabríaishabríais ido
ellos, ellas, ustedeshabríanhabrían ido

The participle never changes: Ella habría ido, Nosotras habríamos ido. The irregular participles are those of the pretérito perfecto: hecho, dicho, visto, escrito, vuelto, puesto, abierto, roto.

Always haber

Good news for English speakers: just as English always says “would have,” Spanish always uses haber, even with verbs of movement and reflexive verbs. “I would have gone” = habría ido; “she would have stayed” = se habría quedado; “we would have gotten up” = nos habríamos levantado.

Pronouns go before habría, and nothing comes between habría and the participle: Lo habría comprado. (I would have bought it.) Me habría quedado. (I would have stayed.)

Don't confuse habría (conditional: “would have”) with había (imperfect: “had”), which you'll practice in the next lesson. One letter changes everything: habría comido = he would have eaten; había comido = he had eaten.

", "

Regrets and reproaches

Expressing a regret

The past conditional says what could have happened but didn't. You don't know the sentence “if I had known…” yet (level B2): replace the condition with a short phrase like con más tiempo, sin ti, en tu lugar or yo que tú.

Habría preferido quedarme en casa.I would have preferred to stay home.
Me habría gustado conocer a tus padres.I would have liked to meet your parents.
Con más tiempo, lo habría hecho mejor.With more time, I would have done it better.
Sin ti, no lo habría conseguido.Without you, I wouldn't have made it.
Yo que tú, habría aceptado la oferta.If I were you, I would have accepted the offer.

Making a reproach

EnglishSpanish
You could have told me!¡Me lo habrías podido decir! / ¡Podrías habérmelo dicho!
You should have called me.Deberías haberme llamado.
You (all) could have let us know.Habríais podido avisar. / Podríais haber avisado.

Haber + participle is the perfect infinitive, like “to have done”: deberías haber llamado = “you should have called.” Pronouns attach to it: haberme llamado, habérmelo dicho (with a written accent, like dímelo).

“You should have” is almost always deberías haber + participle, and “you could have” is podrías haber + participle: the same order as in English. The form “habrías debido” exists, but it sounds clunky.

Regret, miss, be sorry

MeaningSpanishExample
to regret an actionarrepentirse deMe arrepiento de no haber estudiado más.
to miss someone or somethingechar de menosEcho de menos a mis amigos de Lyon.
to be sorrysentirSiento llegar tarde.

He said he would come: the future in the past

As in English, the conditional is also used for the future seen from the past. When the main verb moves into the past, “will” becomes “would”: the future becomes the conditional.

In the presentIn the past
Dice que vendrá. (He says he'll come.)Dijo que vendría. (He said he would come.)
Creo que lloverá. (I think it will rain.)Creía que llovería. (I thought it would rain.)
Sé que te gustará. (I know you'll like it.)Sabía que te gustaría. (I knew you would like it.)

It's very useful for talking about a broken promise or a forecast that turned out wrong:

Me prometió que me llamaría, pero no me llamó.He promised me he would call me, but he didn't.
Pensaba que el viaje sería más barato.I thought the trip would be cheaper.

Simple or past conditional?

  • Simple conditional (“would do”): a wish, advice, a hypothesis about the present or the future. Me gustaría ir. (I'd like to go.)
  • Past conditional (“would have done”): what didn't happen in the past. Me habría gustado ir. (I would have liked to go.)
  • Same logic for advice: Yo que tú, iría (the decision is still ahead) / Yo que tú, habría ido (it's too late).

In Spain, you'll often hear hubiera instead of habría: Hubiera preferido quedarme. Here, both mean the same thing. For now, you just need to recognize it; you'll study this form at level B2.
